# Attainment and transport optimality for median-pair depth

This note gives an attained variational problem and exact finite dual and
swap conditions for the median-pair construction when n=1. It does not
claim that the attained value is at least gamma_d. No log-concavity or
prescribed uniform target law is asserted.

## 1. The compact coupling problem

Let mu be normalized mixed-integer volume on a finite positive-volume
family of convex fibers, and choose an integer median z0. Split the
central fiber proportionally as in `candidate 0b2178fc42ce31d4`, producing
submeasures mu_minus,mu_plus of mass one half with sum mu, supported on
the respective sides z<=z0 and z>=z0. Let

    alpha=2 mu_minus,     beta=2 mu_plus

be probability measures on the compact sets X and Y of source points.
Write Pi(alpha,beta) for their probability couplings.

For p=(i,x), q=(j,x') define the median intersection map by

    T(p,q)=[(j-z0)x+(z0-i)x']/(j-i)       if i<j,
    T(p,q)=(x+x')/2                     if i=j=z0.

Its value belongs to K=C_z0 by convexity. The finitely many integer-index
pair strata are clopen in X times Y, and on each stratum T is affine.
Thus T is continuous, including on the central-central stratum.

Every target probability nu_sigma=T#sigma satisfies

    nu_sigma(H)<=2 mu(H)                              (1)

for every closed ambient halfspace H, with the target identified with its
fiber at z0. This is the endpoint indicator inequality proved in the
transport-route note. It includes boundary mass.

For y in K define

    f_y(sigma)=inf_(u in S^(d-1))
                  sigma{(p,q):u.(T(p,q)-y)>=0},
    V=max_(sigma in Pi(alpha,beta), y in K) f_y(sigma). (2)

Here d>=1; for d=0 every target is the single point and V=1. It suffices
in (2) to use halfspaces through y: every containing closed halfspace
contains its parallel halfspace through y.

The coupling set is weakly compact. Indeed probabilities on a compact
metric space are weakly compact, and the marginal constraints are closed
when tested against continuous functions on X and Y. One elementary proof
of the first assertion extracts a diagonal subsequence on a countable
uniformly dense family of continuous functions; its limits extend to a
positive norm-one functional and hence a probability measure.

The function (sigma,y)->f_y(sigma) is upper semicontinuous. To check this
without assuming that an active direction exists, fix u. If sigma_k tends
weakly to sigma and y_k tends to y, then for each delta>0, eventually

    {u.(T-y_k)>=0} subset {u.(T-y)>=-delta}.

The set on the right is closed. Portmanteau followed by continuity from
above as delta decreases to zero gives

    limsup sigma_k{u.(T-y_k)>=0} <=sigma{u.(T-y)>=0}.

An infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous.
Consequently the maximum in (2) is attained by a single pair (sigma_*,y_*).
This argument permits atoms and never asserts attainment of the infimum
over u. Put v=V=f_(y_*)(sigma_*).

## 2. Finite cap constraints approximate the fixed-center optimum

Fix any y in K and let v_y=max_sigma f_y(sigma). For each epsilon>0
there are finitely many closed halfspaces H_1,...,H_m through y such that

    v_y <= v_F := max_sigma min_i sigma(T^-1 H_i)
                 < v_y+epsilon.                         (3)

To prove this, suppose that for every finite family the constraints
sigma(T^-1 H)>=v_y+epsilon were feasible. Each is a closed subset of the
compact coupling set, by upper semicontinuity of a closed-set mass.
The finite-intersection property would then give one coupling satisfying
all the constraints, contradicting the definition of v_y. The finite
maximum is attained because a finite minimum of closed-set masses is
upper semicontinuous.

The strict inequality in (3) follows from infeasibility at the threshold
v_y+epsilon and attainment. No compactness of the direction-indexed set of
mass values, and no attained smallest cap, is required.

## 3. Exact finite dual and approximate complementarity at the optimizer

For a finite family put c_i(p,q)=1_(H_i)(T(p,q)). Then

    v_F=min_(lambda_i>=0, sum lambda_i=1)
                max_(sigma in Pi(alpha,beta)) integral c_lambda d sigma,
    c_lambda=sum_i lambda_i c_i.                        (4)

Both the outer minimum and the inner maximum are attained. Here is a
finite-dimensional proof. The set

    B={r in R^m: r_i<=integral c_i d sigma for some sigma}

is convex and closed: for a convergent sequence of r choose a weakly
convergent subsequence of its couplings and use upper semicontinuity in
each coordinate. It is closed downward and bounded above coordinatewise.
The point v_F times (1,...,1) is on its upper boundary. Separating B from
(v_F+delta)(1,...,1), normalizing the nonnegative separating coefficients
to sum one, and passing delta to zero gives lambda with

    sup_sigma sum_i lambda_i integral c_i d sigma=v_F.

Nonnegativity follows from downward closure. The reverse inequality follows
from min_i a_i<=sum_i lambda_i a_i. Finally c_lambda is bounded upper
semicontinuous, so its transport maximum is attained. The function of
lambda on the right of (4) is a supremum of continuous affine functions,
and hence lower semicontinuous on the compact simplex; this also proves
attainment of its minimum.

Apply (3),(4) at the maximizing y_*. The original optimizer sigma_* is
epsilon-optimal for this single step-cost transport problem:

    0<=sup_sigma integral c_lambda d sigma
                       -integral c_lambda d sigma_*<epsilon. (5)

It also satisfies the exact weighted approximate activity estimate

    0<=sum_i lambda_i[nu_(sigma_*)(H_i)-v]<epsilon.       (6)

Indeed every cap through y_* has mass at least v, while the dual optimum
v_F is less than v+epsilon. If sigma_F is a finite primal optimizer, then
it is an exact maximizer for c_lambda, and every positive lambda_i has
nu_(sigma_F)(H_i)=v_F. No assertion of a finite exactly active family for
the continuum problem is implicit here.

## 4. Measurable cyclic-swap inequalities, including discontinuous costs

Let c be any bounded Borel cost on X times Y, and let sigma be
epsilon-optimal for its maximization over Pi(alpha,beta). For every
integer k>=2 and every permutation tau of {1,...,k}, put

    Delta=sum_i c(p_i,q_(tau(i)))-sum_i c(p_i,q_i).

Then

    integral (Delta)_+ d sigma^k <= k epsilon.          (7)

For an exact optimizer, Delta<=0 for sigma^k-almost every k-tuple.
This almost-everywhere assertion does not replace sigma's support by a
topologically closed cyclically monotone set.

Proof. For any measurable set A of k-tuples let

    eta_old=(1/k)sum_i (p_i,q_i)#(1_A sigma^k),
    eta_new=(1/k)sum_i (p_i,q_(tau(i)))#(1_A sigma^k).

One has eta_old<=sigma, since each original-coordinate pushforward of the
restricted product measure is at most sigma. The two measures have exactly
the same first and second marginals, because their lists of first and
second coordinates agree pointwise up to permutation. Consequently
sigma'=sigma-eta_old+eta_new is another nonnegative probability coupling.
Its cost gain is (1/k)integral_A Delta d sigma^k. Choose A={Delta>0} and
use epsilon-optimality to obtain (7).

For the optimizing median coupling and the finite dual cost of Section 3,
the especially explicit two-pair consequence is

 integral [sum_i lambda_i(
   1_(H_i)(T(p_1,q_2))+1_(H_i)(T(p_2,q_1))
  -1_(H_i)(T(p_1,q_1))-1_(H_i)(T(p_2,q_2))))]_+
      d sigma_*^2 <=2 epsilon.                          (8)

All swapped pairs remain legal median pairs, since every first endpoint
is in X and every second endpoint is in Y. The pointwise median map still
lands in K. Equations (6),(8) are therefore genuine finite geometric
restrictions on any putative optimizer below gamma_d, with no regularity
assumption on the target or on the cost discontinuity sets.

## 5. What has and has not been obtained

The variational objective is attained; its fixed-center value admits finite
step-cost dual approximations; and its optimizing coupling obeys quantitative
cyclic-swap inequalities for those costs. These statements supply an actual
optimality system rather than merely naming a desired coupling. They do
not prove a gamma_d bound, derive a radial-body structure, or justify any
limiting exact finite active family or continuous transport potentials.

## 6. Why pure deepest-target geometry cannot balance the cap normals

Let A,B,C be the vertices of a nondegenerate triangle and put

    nu=(2/5) delta_A+(3/10) delta_B+(3/10) delta_C.

The unique deepest point is A, of depth 2/5<gamma_2=4/9. At A the atom
gives the lower bound, and a cap isolating A gives equality. If y is any
other point of the triangle, at least one of its B,C barycentric
coordinates is positive. The halfspace where that coordinate is at least
its value at y contains y and exactly the corresponding vertex from the
three support points, so y has depth at most 3/10. Points outside the
triangle have depth zero.

Every cap through A of mass less than 7/10 must exclude both B and C.
Its normal u therefore satisfies

    u.(B-A)<0,      u.(C-A)<0.

All such normals lie in one strict hemisphere, so zero is outside their
convex hull. In particular even arbitrarily accurate active caps cannot
be balanced at the unique deepest point. A secondary choice of center
cannot repair this example.

This target is also realizable by a median coupling of uniform convex
sources. Put a=(1,0), b=(0,1), c=(3/4,3/4), and let

    Z=[0,a]+[0,b]+[0,c].

It tiles, with disjoint interiors, into the parallelograms

    Q1=[0,a]+[0,b],
    Q2=a+[0,b]+[0,c],
    Q3=b+[0,a]+[0,c].

Their areas are 1,3/4,3/4 and sum to area(Z)=5/2. Reflect a uniform
point within its own tile. This is a measure-preserving pairing, whose
midpoint law has the three displayed weights at the noncollinear tile
centers (1/2,1/2),(11/8,7/8),(7/8,11/8). Use it for the outer-outer and
central-central pairs in [-1,1] times Z to obtain the claimed median law.

That coupling is NOT globally optimal: the diagonal pairing gives uniform
measure on Z, whose maximum depth is at least 4/9 by ordinary Grunbaum.
Thus the obstruction excludes reasoning based only on an arbitrary deepest
target; it does not exclude an additional consequence of actual coupling
optimality.
